title: At the café
goal: Order drinks and snacks, ask for the bill, and fit in Romanian's most distinctive feature: the definite article glued to the end of the noun — *the* placed behind.
bekal: order politely with *aș vrea…* and *…, vă rog*, and know when *vreau* sounds too blunt
give any singular noun its definite article: *-ul, -l, -le, -a, -ua*
ask for a recommendation, ask for the bill, and pay by card

dialogs.title: Dialogue — La o cafenea în Centrul Vechi
dialogs.intro: Saturday afternoon. Ioana takes Budi to a café in Centrul Vechi, the old town of București. A waiter comes over to their table.

notes: **O cafea, then cafeaua.** When ordering, the coffee doesn't exist yet and isn't specific: *o cafea* — "a coffee". Once the cup is on the table, it becomes *cafeaua* — "the coffee". Likewise *un ceai → ceaiul*. That's exactly where English also switches from "a" to "the", and it's the point of this unit.

**Aș vrea is softer than vreau.** Ioana, ordering from the waiter, uses *aș vrea* ("I'd like"). Budi uses *vreau* — but he's stating his taste, not giving an order, and he closes with *vă rog*. Details in the second grammar box.

**Ce îmi recomandați? — learn it whole.** *Îmi* means "to me", and the waiter answers with its partner: *Vă recomand…* ("I recommend to you…"). Small pronouns like these come in units 10 and 19; for now, the ready-made sentence is enough.

**Pot să plătesc…? is a chunk too.** *Pot să* + verb = "can I / may I…". The *să* construction arrives in unit 11. Notice *cu cardul*: after *cu*, the noun keeps its article — the opposite of most other prepositions, as unit 6 explains.

**Poftiți and Poftă bună.** *Poftiți* is the polite form of *poftim* (unit 1): "here you are". *Poftă bună* literally means "good appetite" and is said before eating by anyone at the table — including the waiter to the guests. The reply is *Mulțumesc, la fel!* ("Thanks, you too!").

grammars.title: The definite article — an ending glued on behind
body: English puts *the* in front. Romanian — alone among its Latin sisters — glues it **behind** the noun as an ending: *cafeaua* = "coffee-the", *nota* = "bill-the". Which ending you use depends on the gender and the last letter of the word.

head: Gender and ending
Ending
Indefinite
Definite
rows: **m / n** ending in a consonant or *-i*

after: **Now the puzzle from unit 3 is solved.** *Mama mea, sora mea, familia mea* use the ending *-a*; *fratele meu* uses *-le*; *copilul meu* and *soțul meu* use *-ul*. A possessive demands the definite article, so the ending is always there. Two irregular forms to memorize: *tată → tatăl* and *zi → ziua* (hence *bună ziua*).

**When is it used?** Almost always where English uses *the*: things already mentioned or clear to both sides (*Nota, vă rog*), and nouns that are the topic of the sentence (*Cafeaua este bună*). Romanian also uses it for general statements where English has no article: *Cafeaua e scumpă aici* = "Coffee is expensive here". **When not?** After *un / o*, after *a fi* + job, and after most prepositions (unit 6).

**What you'll hear on the street.** In fast speech, the *l* of *-ul* is almost always swallowed: *cardul* sounds like "kardoo", *ceaiul* like "chah-yoo". In writing the *l* is required; for your ear, the *-u* at the end is enough to signal the article.

grammars.title: Vreau versus aș vrea — want and would like
body: *A vrea* (to want) is irregular, but short. Next to it stands its softer form — the conditional — used every time you ask a stranger for something.
after: **The difference is exactly "I want a coffee" versus "I'd like a coffee".** *Vreau o cafea* to a waiter isn't grammatically wrong, but it sounds like a child making demands. *Aș vrea o cafea* is always safe. Just as polite: *Aș dori o cafea*. And even the simplest version is polite, as long as you close with the magic word: *O cafea, vă rog.*
**Among friends, *vreau* and *vrei* are perfectly normal**: *Vrei o cafea? — Da, vreau.* What's rude isn't the verb but using it to give orders to someone serving you.

**For now, use *a vrea* only with nouns**: *Vreau un ceai*, *Vrem nota*. If what you want is an action — "I want to pay" — Romanian needs *să*: *Vreau să plătesc*. That's the point of unit 11. You only need to recognize the polite-form column; the one to memorize is *aș vrea*.

blocks.text: If you order water, the waiter will ask back: *Plată sau minerală?* — *apă plată* is still water, *apă minerală* sparkling. And if you just order *o cafea*, what arrives is usually an espresso; for coffee with milk, ask for *o cafea cu lapte* or simply say *un cappuccino*.

blocks.title: Three things worth tasting
items: **Papanași** — fried doughnuts made from fresh cheese dough (*brânză de vaci*), served warm with sour cream (*smântână*) and berry jam. Almost every Romanian restaurant has them; one portion is usually enough for two.
**Covrigi** — pretzel rings topped with sesame, poppy seeds, or coarse salt, sold warm at *covrigărie* kiosks on almost every corner of București. Cheap, and breakfast on the go for half the city.

**Cafea la ibric** — ground coffee boiled in a small long-handled copper pot and poured out with its grounds. It's the old Romanian way of making coffee at home, and the most familiar to anyone who loves Turkish coffee.

sections.title: Café phrases, from sitting down to paying

head: Sentence
English
rows: Do you have a free table?
We'll pay together. / We'll pay separately.

blocks.text: Notice how often the definite article appears in this table: *meniul, nota, cardul, restul*. They're all things already clear to you and the waiter — there's only one menu, one bill, one change. On the other hand, *o masă liberă* and *o cafea* are indefinite, because any one will do. *Nu mănânc carne de porc* uses a verb that only arrives in unit 7; learn it whole, since Romanian cooking uses a lot of pork and you may need it from day one.

blocks.title: Two table customs worth knowing
items: **Bacșiș** (the tip) isn't included in the price and is usually about ten percent. Many restaurants print a separate *bacșiș* line on the bill, so you can add it even when paying by card. When paying cash, name a round amount or say *Păstrați restul*.
**Noroc!** is what you say when clinking glasses — literally "luck!". Romanians look each other in the eye as the glasses touch. A more formal toast: *Sănătate!* ("health!").
